question: Why does gradient descent not guarantee finding the global minimum in neural networks?
direct_answer: Because the loss surface is usually nonconvex, so gradient descent can get stuck in local minima, saddle points, or flat regions.
expanded_answer: In convex optimization, any local minimum is global, but neural network loss landscapes are generally nonconvex and high-dimensional. That means gradient descent may converge to different solutions depending on initialization, learning rate, and stochasticity. It may also slow down near saddle points or flat plateaus where gradients are small even though the point is not optimal.
key_points: Neural network losses are typically nonconvex
Local minima are not necessarily global minima
Saddle points and flat regions can slow progress
Initialization and stochasticity affect the outcome
common_wrong_ideas: Gradient descent always finds the best possible model
If loss decreases, the optimizer must be near the global minimum
Only local minima matter; saddle points do not
